title: Cost-of-living clashes in Brussels and Liege
deck: Belgian students copied France's school blockades, the marches turned to clashes with police on 17 October, and a budget deadlock has since left the prime minister offering to resign.

whatHappened: On 17 October 2026, police clashed with demonstrators in Brussels and Liege. The clashes came after weeks of high-school protests in Belgium that echoed France's. Belgium's interior minister called it violence, not protest.

The Belgian wave copied France. French students had blockaded schools over teacher shortages. Belgian students took up the same blockades and similar demands weeks later. That grew into cost-of-living marches.

On 2 November, Prime Minister Bart De Wever offered his resignation after failing to pass the federal budget. The king deferred a decision. The same day, French students were reported blocking schools for a third week on a smaller scale.
whyItMatters: Politics and protest: Belgium is a case of copycat unrest. French blockades are still going, so the example is still in front of Belgian students. We do not have turnout or arrest figures for Belgium, so the scale is unclear. It looks smaller than in France.

Living costs: the marches carried a cost-of-living message. Euronews framed the European wave as a wages-versus-prices squeeze. That makes the anger hard to settle with one concession, because it is broader than one school policy.

Security: the interior minister's choice of words, violence and not protest, suggests a policing response first. That can harden the movement or thin it out. Both have happened in past European unrest.

Budget: the prime minister's offer to resign over the budget is not proven to be caused by the protests. But it lands at the worst time. A government that cannot pass a budget has little room to answer demands for relief.

predict.question: Before you read the scenarios: what is the most likely path for Belgium over the next two months?
predict.explanation: Our base case, at about 40%, is that the French wave fades, Belgian street protests thin out, and the budget and the king's decision become the main story. A political crisis with protests as a side issue is next at about 30%.

timeline.title: French school blockades begin
timeline.detail: Students at a Paris-suburb high school blockade over teacher shortages. The tactic spreads across France. Belgian students later copy it.

timeline.title: 550,000 march in France
timeline.detail: About 550,000 marched in France and roughly 2,400 were arrested in one day. Unrest spreads to other European cities the same weekend.

timeline.title: Police clash with demonstrators in Brussels and Liege
timeline.detail: The clashes follow weeks of Belgian high-school protests that echoed France's.

timeline.title: Interior minister calls it violence, not protest
timeline.detail: The framing signals a security-first response rather than negotiation.

timeline.title: Euronews explains the economic pressures behind the protests
timeline.detail: The analysis sets wages against prices as a driver of unrest across several European countries.

timeline.title: French school protests resume on a smaller scale
timeline.detail: Students return from break and keep blocking school entrances for a third week. The government warns against blockades.

timeline.title: Belgian PM offers to resign over the budget
timeline.detail: Bart De Wever offers his resignation after failing to pass the federal budget. The king defers a decision.

timeline.title: Wider European unrest is the subject of analysis
timeline.detail: Outlets such as SBS run explainers on the growing unrest across Europe and its causes.

causes.name: Prices versus wages
causes.detail: Euronews points to cost-of-living pressure, with prices outpacing pay in several countries, as a base of the protests. Belgium-specific numbers were not available to us.

causes.name: Strained public budgets
causes.detail: Belgium's federal budget could not be passed, which shows how little fiscal room there is. The size of the gap is not in our sources.

causes.name: Youth distrust
causes.detail: Commentary in the wire coverage suggests young people feel unheard. This is opinion, not measured fact.

causes.name: French school blockades
causes.detail: French students blockaded schools over teacher shortages. Belgian students copied the method and similar demands.

causes.name: Marches on 17 October
causes.detail: The Belgian school protests turned into cost-of-living marches in Brussels and Liege.

causes.name: Police confrontation
causes.detail: Clashes with police in two cities on 17 October drew the interior minister's violence, not protest, response.

causes.name: Budget deadlock
causes.detail: The PM's offer to resign adds political instability. We have not seen proof that it was caused by the protests.

causes.name: Continuing French example
causes.detail: French blockades entered a third week, so the trigger is still active, although smaller.

stakeholders.name: Belgian students and youth organisers
stakeholders.wants: Better school conditions and relief from cost-of-living pressure, copying French demands
stakeholders.leverage: Blockades and marches; media attention after 17 October
stakeholders.likelyMove: Keep protesting if France does; fade if France fades

stakeholders.name: Belgium's interior minister
stakeholders.wants: Public order, and to define the clashes as violence rather than legitimate protest
stakeholders.leverage: Police powers and the framing of events
stakeholders.likelyMove: Hold a firm line on violence; avoid concessions framed as a reward for clashes

stakeholders.name: Prime Minister Bart De Wever
stakeholders.wants: A federal budget passed and a government that survives
stakeholders.leverage: Control of the coalition and the budget process; the resignation offer is also a bargaining move
stakeholders.likelyMove: Seek a deal with coalition partners or step aside if the king accepts

stakeholders.name: The king
stakeholders.role: Head of state, arbiter of government crises
stakeholders.wants: A stable government without being seen as taking sides
stakeholders.leverage: Power to accept or defer the resignation and to start consultations
stakeholders.likelyMove: Consult party leaders; a decision is pending, with no date given

stakeholders.name: Police and city authorities in Brussels and Liege
stakeholders.wants: Avoid injuries and damage in city centres
stakeholders.leverage: Crowd control and decisions on authorising marches
stakeholders.likelyMove: Tighter control of future march routes; arrests for violence

stakeholders.name: French students and government
stakeholders.wants: Students: school staffing and funding. Government: an end to blockades
stakeholders.leverage: French blockades are the model Belgian students copied
stakeholders.likelyMove: Blockades continue on a smaller scale; the government warns against them

stakeholders.name: Wider European protest networks
stakeholders.wants: A hearing on the cost of living and a say in policy
stakeholders.leverage: Shared methods and media coverage across borders
stakeholders.likelyMove: Further copycat action wherever grievances match

sectors.why: The federal budget failed to pass and the PM has offered to resign. Uncertainty delays spending and tax decisions.
Blockades disrupt lessons. The scale in Belgium is unknown.

sectors.sector: Retail and hospitality in Brussels and Liege centres
sectors.why: Clashes keep shoppers away on protest days. We have no damage figures, so this is an estimate.

sectors.sector: Transport and logistics in city centres
sectors.why: Marches can close roads and stations for hours. Effects are local and short.
A firm line on violence means more police deployment on protest days; demand for security services tends to follow.

dailyLife.effect: Marches can close streets and disrupt transport around central squares on protest days. No new march is confirmed.
The protests are tied to a wages-versus-prices squeeze. We have no Belgian figures; see the Euronews analysis for the wider picture.
Blockades or disruption may reach more schools if the French example continues. French blockades were in a third week on 2 November.

scenarios.name: Fading echo
scenarios.looksLike: French blockades thin out, Belgian street action fades, and the budget and the king's decision dominate the news.
signposts: Smaller turnout at any Belgian march
scenarios.effectOnWorld: The unrest remains a footnote. European attention goes back to budgets and prices.

scenarios.name: Political crisis first
scenarios.looksLike: The king accepts the resignation or the coalition is reshaped. Protests become a side issue to government formation.
signposts: Coalition partners trade public blame over the budget
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Belgium is distracted for weeks or months. Belgian EU policy positions may be harder to read.

scenarios.name: Renewed street wave
scenarios.looksLike: New marches in Brussels and Liege with more clashes, helped by political chaos and continuing French action.
signposts: A new march date is announced
Injuries or serious damage in city centres
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Copycat action in neighbouring countries becomes more likely; businesses face more disruption.

scenarios.name: Quick budget fix
scenarios.looksLike: A budget deal is reached fast, with some relief measures, and the PM stays.
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Calm returns in Belgium. The French wave runs on separately.

confidence.note: Taken from the event summary and the Euronews analysis. We did not have the underlying police or ministry statements.

confidence.note: From the judged connection to the France dossier; no Belgian-specific source was opened. France's 550,000 marchers and 2,400 arrests come from the same connection.

confidence.note: Reported in a Le Monde headline dated 2 November; we saw the headline, not the full article.

confidence.claim: The budget impasse and the protests are linked

evidence.method: Drafted from the four listed sources, the event summary, the judged connection to the France dossier and 21 wire headlines matched on 2 November 2026. Several sources were seen as headlines or short summaries only. Belgian turnout, arrests, damage and economic numbers were not available and are not estimated. Scenario probabilities, predictions and the analogue comparisons are the author's judgement or general knowledge.
